story: In November 1967, Cambridge graduate student Jocelyn Bell Burnell detected a repeating radio signal using the Interplanetary Scintillation Array. Flashing every 1.337 seconds with precision, the signal originated from the constellation Vulpecula. Because of its unnaturally steady beat, Bell Burnell and supervisor Antony Hewish initially nicknamed the source LGM-1, short for Little Green Men, wondering if it was an alien radio beacon. The emission was soon identified as CP 1919, a rapidly rotating neutron star emitting periodic radio beams—the very first pulsar ever discovered. Although Hewish was awarded the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery without Bell Burnell, sparking controversy, she later received the $3 million Breakthrough Prize in 2018. In 1979, a stacked plot of CP 1919's pulses created by radio astronomer Harold Craft became the iconic album cover for Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures.
angle: The first discovered pulsar flashed with such unnatural 1.337-second precision that scientists initially cataloged it as an alien beacon named LGM-1.
disputed: The precision of the 1.337302088331-second rotation period: sources note this 12-decimal figure was measured in 1991 rather than in 1967. A script should state the period simply as 1.337 seconds.

Supervisory credit vs co-discovery credit for the Nobel Prize: astronomer Fred Hoyle argued Bell Burnell should have shared the 1974 Nobel Prize. A script should attribute this opinion as 'according to astronomer Fred Hoyle'.
